awd_titl_txt: RAPID: Impact of Back-to-Back Major Hurricanes on Antibiotic Resistance Gene Transfer to Autochthonous Bacteria in Estuarine and Coastal Water Systems
awd_abstract_narration:
Hurricanes cause severe damages to infrastructure, polluting coastal water, and disrupting the environment and human health. This research studies flooding-caused pollution in west Florida coastal waters after two major hurricanes. The project will understand how land bacteria transfer antibiotic resistant genes to coastal bacteria during flooding. The team will analyze water samples collected after the hurricanes using microbiological, chemical and molecular methods. The outcomes of this study will enhance our understanding of how marine pathogens, like vibrios, acquire toxic traits and pose threats to public health. The results will provide valuable data in guiding emergency responses in the face of future storms.

The recent back-to-back hurricanes in Florida, Helene and Milton, caused extensive flooding that released untreated wastewater carrying antibiotic resistant genes (ARGs) from freshwater environments into coastal waters. The spread of ARGs into marine ecosystems poses a significant public health threat, as it can lead to the emergence of antibiotic resistant marine bacteria, including species such as Vibrio vulnificus, a pathogen associated with severe and sometimes fatal infections. This project will investigate how storm-driven flooding facilitates the horizontal transfer of ARGs between freshwater and marine bacteria, contributing to the long-term persistence of ARGs in coastal ecosystems. Key objectives include identifying antibiotic resistant freshwater bacteria entering coastal waters, examining the horizontal transfer of ARGs within biofilms in coastal waters, and assessing the persistence of ARGs in marine bacteria over time. Samples collected after the hurricanes will be analyzed using long-read metagenomics, single-colony sequencing, and microbial community analysis to track bacterial origins and resolve ARG profiles, as well as stable isotope analysis to differentiate freshwater and marine bacterial populations. This study will highlight how hurricanes amplify the risks of ARGs entering marine ecosystems and conferring antibiotic resistance to pathogens. These pathogens can impact public health through seafood consumption, recreational exposure, or environmental contact. The findings will provide critical insights into mitigating the long-term effects of hurricanes on public health and coastal water quality, while informing strategies to reduce the spread of antibiotic resistance in marine environments.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This NSF RAPID project investigated how Hurricane Milton affected microbial water quality in estuarine and coastal waters in Florida. The project focused on whether storm surge, flooding, runoff, wastewater releases, and resuspended coastal materials transported microbial threats into coastal environments. These microbial threats included fecal indicator bacteria, opportunistic pathogens, and antimicrobial resistance genes. The attached illustration (Fig. 1) summarizes the central question of the project: after a tropical cyclone, do microbial threats in coastal waters come from terrestrial runoff, wastewater sources, marine sources, or a combination of these pathways?

To answer this question, the project collected water and particle samples along approximately 150 km of Florida’s Gulf Coast after Hurricane Milton. Sampling locations included the Cape Coral–Fort Myers region, the Caloosahatchee River system, adjacent coastal waters, Tampa Bay, and other hurricane-impacted coastal areas. Samples were collected shortly after the hurricane, including 1–2 weeks after the event, and again 7 months later to compare short-term hurricane impacts with longer-term recovery conditions.

The project used multiple analytical approaches. Microplastics were separated by size, including particles larger and smaller than 25 µm, and were characterized using stereomicroscopy and pyrolysis-gas chromatography/mass spectrometry. Microbial targets were quantified using digital PCR, including total bacteria, E. coli, Pseudomonas, Vibrio spp., and several antimicrobial resistance genes. Bacterial communities were analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and untargeted metagenomic analysis was used to identify antimicrobial resistance genes and virulence factors associated with particles.

The project produced several important findings. First, conventional fecal indicator bacteria did not fully represent the persistence of microbial threats after Hurricane Milton. Enterococci levels declined rapidly within approximately two weeks after the hurricane, which could suggest apparent water-quality recovery. However, other microbial indicators, including antimicrobial resistance genes, Pseudomonas, Vibrio spp., and total bacterial signals, showed different recovery patterns. This finding suggests that post-hurricane water-quality monitoring based only on fecal indicator bacteria may underestimate the duration and complexity of microbial risks.

Second, the project showed that hurricanes can substantially alter microplastic contamination in coastal waters. Microplastic concentrations were significantly higher after the hurricane than 7 months later. Smaller microplastics were generally more abundant than larger particles, and post-hurricane samples showed changes in polymer composition, including the detection of denser plastics such as PVC and PMMA at some locations.

Third, the project demonstrated that microplastics can help transport inland-derived bacteria into marine environments. Particles larger than 25 µm contained approximately 86% inland-derived bacteria, which was higher than the proportion observed in surrounding water. Laboratory experiments showed that inland-derived bacteria survived approximately 80% longer when attached to microplastics as biofilms than when they were free-floating in seawater. These particle-associated inland bacteria contributed approximately 25% of the antimicrobial resistance genes introduced into coastal environments during the hurricane event.

Fourth, the project developed a new computational framework called Large-Language-Model-Assisted Microbial Habitat Assessment, or LAMHA. LAMHA uses microbial sequencing data, public biological databases, and large language models to infer whether bacteria are likely from terrestrial, wastewater, or marine sources. Using this approach, the project found that different microbial threats were linked to different sources. For example, the sul2 antimicrobial resistance gene was associated with terrestrial sources, the tetA gene was associated with wastewater sources, and Vibrio parahaemolyticus was associated with marine sources.

The project also provided research training for three undergraduate students and one graduate student. Students gained experience in rapid-response field sampling, filtration, DNA extraction, digital PCR, fecal indicator bacteria analysis, microplastic analysis, sequencing data analysis, microbial source tracking, statistics, and data visualization.

Overall, this project showed that hurricanes can introduce microbial threats into coastal waters through multiple pathways, and that the quantitative contribution of each pathway can be resolved by combining microbial community analysis with large language models. The project also showed that microplastics can extend the persistence of inland-derived microbial threats in coastal environments (Fig. 2). These findings can help coastal managers and public health agencies improve post-hurricane water-quality monitoring by considering antimicrobial resistance genes, pathogens, microplastics, and microbial source information in addition to conventional fecal indicator bacteria.
